name: Applied Materials, Inc.
domainRelevance: Applied Materials is the world's largest semiconductor equipment manufacturer, supplying critical process tools for wafer fabrication across all technology nodes from mature to cutting-edge. Its equipment portfolio spans deposition, etch, implant, and metrology systems that enable chip makers to achieve yield and performance targets. As the primary capital equipment supplier to TSMC, Samsung, Intel, and Chinese foundries, AMAT's order book and backlog serve as a leading indicator of semiconductor industry capex cycles and geopolitical supply-chain shifts.
portalRelevance: AMAT is a tier-1 anchor in the semiconductor supply chain and a critical bellwether for technology sector capital intensity. Its quarterly revenue, gross margin, and order-book guidance directly forecast foundry utilization and chip-maker profitability 2–4 quarters forward. Export controls on China-bound equipment and fab construction cycles in Taiwan, South Korea, and the U.S. create regulatory and geopolitical leverage points that move AMAT's valuation and risk profile independently of broader market sentiment.

intelligenceCycle.name: Signal Capture
items: Quarterly orders and backlog disclosures in 10-Q/10-K filings; backlog-to-revenue ratio as leading indicator of 2–3 quarter demand visibility
Gross margin and operating leverage trends; equipment ASP (average selling price) deflation or inflation tied to node transition and competitive intensity
8-K filings on major customer wins (e.g., TSMC advanced node capacity announcements, Intel foundry services ramp) and supply-chain disruptions
Export control and tariff announcements affecting China revenue (currently ~25–30% of total per 10-K Item 1A); geopolitical risk repricing

intelligenceCycle.name: State Estimation
items: Phase classification tied to semiconductor capex cycle: P0–P2 (contraction, order cancellations, margin compression) vs P7–P10 (expansion, record orders, pricing power)
Free cash flow trajectory: capex intensity for R&D (15–18% of revenue) and working capital swings tied to customer payment terms and inventory build
Debt-to-EBITDA and interest coverage; AMAT maintains investment-grade rating but faces refinancing risk if capex cycle turns sharply
Customer concentration risk: TSMC + Samsung + Intel represent ~60–70% of revenue; loss of any one customer creates material downside

intelligenceCycle.name: Diagnosis
items: Pattern match: semiconductor capex peak-to-trough cycles (2018, 2022–23) correlate with AMAT revenue swings of ±30–40%; current cycle inflection point tied to AI/data-center fab buildout
Competitive pressure from Tokyo Electron (TYE) and Lam Research (LRCX) in etch/deposition; AMAT's market share erosion in specific process nodes signals technology lag or customer defection
Geopolitical contagion: U.S. export controls on China-bound equipment (2023–24) created $2–3B revenue headwind; recovery depends on policy reversal or China domestic tool adoption
Margin compression signature: gross margin below 45% for 2+ quarters signals pricing pressure, product mix shift to lower-ASP tools, or manufacturing inefficiency

intelligenceCycle.name: Regulation
items: Investment thesis: long AMAT if backlog-to-revenue ratio >1.5 and customer capex guidance accelerating (AI fab ramp); short if ratio <1.0 and gross margin trending below 42%
Risk hedge: long semiconductor equipment ETF (SMH) to hedge single-name concentration; short Taiwan currency (TWD) to hedge TSMC revenue concentration and geopolitical Taiwan risk
Engagement strategy: monitor quarterly earnings calls for customer commentary on fab utilization, node transitions, and capex timing; flag any guidance cut as phase-transition signal
Regulatory watch: track BIS (Bureau of Industry and Security) export control updates on China; model revenue impact scenarios for 0%, 25%, 50% China revenue loss

intelligenceCycle.name: Action
items: Trade execution: initiate long position on AMAT if backlog growth >20% YoY and gross margin guidance stable or improving; size 3–5% of portfolio given capex-cycle volatility
Rebalancing: reduce AMAT exposure if orders decline 2 consecutive quarters or customer concentration (top-3) exceeds 75%; rotate proceeds to diversified semiconductor suppliers
Engagement: attend quarterly earnings call and investor day; request management color on customer capex plans, China revenue trajectory, and gross margin recovery path
Monitoring setup: track weekly semiconductor equipment billings (SEMI data), monthly Taiwan fab utilization rates, and monthly U.S. fab construction starts as leading indicators

intelligenceCycle.name: Feedback
items: Earnings validation: compare Q+1 orders guidance vs. prior quarter backlog; if orders miss guidance by >10%, flag as phase-transition warning
Price action: monitor AMAT stock reaction to earnings; if stock declines >10% on in-line earnings, suggests market repricing capex cycle expectations downward
Filing delta: review 10-Q Item 1A risk factors for new or expanded China revenue disclosure, customer concentration changes, or supply-chain disruption language
Peer comparison: benchmark AMAT gross margin, order backlog, and free cash flow vs. Tokyo Electron and Lam Research; divergence signals competitive share loss or gain

intelligenceCycle.name: Adaptation
items: Model update: recalibrate phase-transition thresholds based on realized backlog-to-revenue ratios; if current cycle peak is higher than 2018 or 2022, adjust P10 ceiling upward
Signal reweight: if China export control announcements move AMAT stock >5% intraday, increase weight on geopolitical risk signals in next quarter's kernel run
Sector prior update: if AMAT margin compression precedes broader semiconductor peer margin compression by 1–2 quarters, increase AMAT's role as leading indicator in sector model
Customer concentration sensitivity: if TSMC revenue share exceeds 35%, increase downside scenario weighting for Taiwan geopolitical risk in portfolio stress tests

functionalNetwork.model: Applied Materials operates as a capital-equipment orchestrator at the center of the semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem. Its business model mirrors a decision-making hub: it receives demand signals from foundries and IDMs (integrated device manufacturers) via customer capex guidance and fab construction plans; translates those signals into equipment orders and R&D roadmaps; executes manufacturing and delivery of complex process tools; and feeds back performance data (yield, throughput, defect rates) to customers, creating a tight feedback loop that drives next-generation tool specifications. AMAT's gross margin, order backlog, and customer concentration metrics serve as leading indicators of semiconductor industry health, making it a critical node in the technology sector's financial-intelligence network.

suppliers.name: Tokyo Electron Limited
suppliers.relationshipNote: Japanese competitor with ~20% global market share in etch and deposition; strong in mature-node and specialty process tools. TYE has maintained pricing discipline and higher gross margins (48–52%) vs. AMAT (42–48%) by focusing on lower-volume, higher-ASP specialty segments. TYE's partnership with TSMC on advanced node tools creates competitive threat in AMAT's core market. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 industry overview and competitive analysis.

suppliers.name: KLA Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Dominant metrology and inspection tool supplier; ~60% market share in wafer inspection. KLAC is not a direct competitor in deposition/etch but is a complementary supplier in the fab tool ecosystem. AMAT and KLAC often bundle tools in customer proposals; KLAC's margin profile (58–62% gross margin) and order visibility exceed AMAT's, signaling stronger customer demand for inspection tools relative to process tools. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 and quarterly earnings calls.

suppliers.name: ASML Holding N.V.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Dutch lithography equipment leader; ~90% market share in advanced node lithography (EUV). ASML is not a direct competitor to AMAT but is a critical upstream supplier in the fab tool chain. ASML's EUV tool delivery delays (2022–23) created bottlenecks that reduced demand for AMAT's downstream etch and deposition tools. ASML's export control restrictions (Dutch government limits China sales) create geopolitical leverage that affects AMAT's China revenue indirectly. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A risk factors.

suppliers.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited
suppliers.relationshipNote: Largest customer; represents ~30–35% of AMAT revenue (disclosed in 10-K Item 1A). TSMC's capex guidance (typically $25–30B annually) directly drives AMAT orders 1–2 quarters forward. TSMC's advanced node (3nm, 2nm) roadmap requires next-generation AMAT tools; AMAT has secured design-win commitments for TSMC's N3 and N2 nodes. TSMC's Taiwan geopolitical risk (U.S.–China tensions, potential military conflict) creates binary downside scenario for AMAT revenue. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A customer concentration and quarterly earnings calls.

suppliers.name: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Second-largest customer; represents ~20–25% of AMAT revenue. Samsung's foundry business (Samsung Foundry Services) is ramping advanced nodes (3nm, 2nm) to compete with TSMC; this capex cycle is driving record AMAT orders for Samsung in 2023–24. Samsung's South Korea fab expansion (Pyeongtaek, Hwaseong) requires significant AMAT tool purchases. Samsung's memory business (DRAM, NAND) is cyclical; memory capex downturns reduce AMAT orders by 15–20%. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A and quarterly earnings calls.

suppliers.name: China Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation
suppliers.relationshipNote: Leading Chinese foundry; represents ~5–8% of AMAT revenue but is subject to U.S. export control restrictions (BIS Entity List since 2020). SMIC's capex plans are constrained by inability to purchase advanced AMAT tools (EUV-capable systems); SMIC is forced to use older-node AMAT tools or domestic Chinese alternatives. U.S. export control policy changes directly impact AMAT's China revenue; each new restriction reduces AMAT China revenue by $200–500M annually. SMIC's technology roadmap (28nm, 14nm focus) is 3–5 years behind TSMC/Samsung, limiting AMAT's advanced-tool sales to China. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A China risk factors and 8-K filings on export control announcements.

suppliers.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: Major memory (DRAM, NAND) manufacturer; represents ~3–5% of AMAT revenue. Micron's capex cycles are highly volatile; memory capex downturns (2022–23) reduced AMAT orders by 20–30%. Micron's new U.S. fab construction (Idaho, Texas) is driving AMAT orders for memory-specific tools (deposition, etch) in 2024–25. Micron's gross margin compression (2022–23) led to capex deferrals; recovery depends on DRAM/NAND pricing recovery. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A and quarterly earnings calls.

suppliers.name: SK Hynix Inc.
suppliers.relationshipNote: South Korean memory manufacturer; represents ~2–4% of AMAT revenue. SK Hynix's capex is tied to DRAM/NAND market cycles; memory downturns reduce AMAT orders. SK Hynix's South Korea fab expansion (Icheon, Cheonan) is driving AMAT tool purchases for advanced memory nodes. SK Hynix's partnership with Intel on memory technology (2021–22) created incremental AMAT orders for joint development tools. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A and quarterly earnings calls.

suppliers.name: DHL Supply Chain
suppliers.relationshipNote: Primary logistics partner for AMAT equipment shipments to Asia-Pacific fabs (TSMC, Samsung, SMIC). DHL manages complex customs clearance, export control compliance, and on-time delivery of large, sensitive semiconductor tools. AMAT's equipment is high-value, fragile, and subject to export control regulations; DHL's expertise in export compliance and Taiwan/South Korea logistics is critical to AMAT's supply chain. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 supply chain overview.

suppliers.name: Kuehne+Nagel International AG
suppliers.relationshipNote: Global logistics partner for AMAT equipment shipments to U.S. and European fabs. Kuehne+Nagel manages customs clearance, export control compliance, and on-time delivery of AMAT tools to Intel, GlobalFoundries, and other U.S. foundries. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 supply chain overview.

logisticsPartners.name: Nippon Express Co., Ltd.
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Japanese logistics partner for AMAT equipment shipments to Japan and South Korea fabs. Nippon Express specializes in semiconductor equipment logistics and has established relationships with AMAT's Japanese customers (Tokyo Electron, Sony Semiconductor). Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 supply chain overview.

logisticsPartners.name: Panalpina (now part of DSV)
logisticsPartners.relationshipNote: Logistics partner for AMAT equipment shipments to China fabs (SMIC, CXMT). DSV/Panalpina manages export control compliance for China-bound equipment; critical to AMAT's ability to navigate U.S. export restrictions and deliver tools to approved Chinese customers. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A China risk factors.

customers.name: GlobalFoundries Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: U.S.-based foundry; represents ~3–5% of AMAT revenue. GlobalFoundries' capex is focused on mature-node (28nm, 14nm) and specialty process (RF, analog) tools; lower ASP than advanced-node tools but stable demand. GlobalFoundries' U.S. fab expansion (Malta, New York; Dresden, Germany) is driving AMAT orders for mature-node deposition and etch tools. GlobalFoundries' gross margin (35–40%) is lower than TSMC/Samsung, limiting capex spending. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A and quarterly earnings calls.

customers.name: UMC (United Microelectronics Corporation)
customers.relationshipNote: Taiwan-based foundry; represents ~2–3% of AMAT revenue. UMC's capex is focused on mature-node and specialty process tools; lower ASP than TSMC. UMC's partnership with Hua Hong Semiconductor (China JV) creates indirect exposure to China market and export control risk. UMC's gross margin (25–30%) is lower than TSMC, limiting capex spending. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A and quarterly earnings calls.

customers.name: Alphabet Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Alphabet drives indirect semiconductor equipment demand through its AI infrastructure capex cycle. As a hyperscaler customer of foundries like TSMC and Samsung, Alphabet's advanced-chip requirements cascade into orders for Applied Materials' deposition and lithography-support systems. Its AI monetization trajectory and cloud-capex intensity signal multi-year demand sustainability for next-generation process nodes.

customers.name: Broadcom Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Broadcom sources advanced-node semiconductor manufacturing equipment from Applied Materials through foundry partnerships at TSMC and Samsung. As a fabless chip designer with outsized exposure to hyperscaler and telecom capex cycles, Broadcom's design wins for AI and 5G infrastructure directly translate into equipment orders. Lead times and process complexity create forward visibility into Applied Materials' revenue.

customers.name: Meta Platforms, Inc.
customers.relationshipNote: Meta's substantial annual capex for custom AI chips drives indirect demand for Applied Materials' semiconductor equipment at foundry partners TSMC and Samsung. As a hyperscaler with sustained infrastructure investment, Meta's chip roadmap signals multi-year equipment demand across deposition, etch, and metrology. Its capex trajectory remains a leading indicator of semiconductor manufacturing intensity.

customers.name: Intel Corporation
customers.relationshipNote: Third-largest customer; represents ~10–15% of AMAT revenue. Intel's foundry services (IFS) capex ramp (2023–24) is driving AMAT orders for advanced node tools at Intel's Arizona and Ohio fabs. Intel's process technology roadmap (Intel 4, Intel 3, Intel 20A) requires next-generation AMAT deposition and etch tools. Intel's gross margin pressure (2022–23) led to capex cuts that reduced AMAT orders; recovery depends on IFS customer wins and process node yield improvements. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A and quarterly earnings calls.

competitors.name: Lam Research Corporation
competitors.relationshipNote: Direct competitor in etch and deposition process tools; LRCX holds ~25–30% market share in etch vs. AMAT's ~40–45%. LRCX has gained share in advanced node etch (5nm and below) over past 3 years, signaling technology parity or superiority in specific process windows. Competitive pricing pressure from LRCX on ASP (average selling price) has compressed AMAT gross margin by 100–150 bps since 2021. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A competitive risk factors and quarterly earnings call commentary.

competitors.name: Tokyo Electron Limited
competitors.relationshipNote: Japanese competitor with ~20% global market share in etch and deposition; strong in mature-node and specialty process tools. TYE has maintained pricing discipline and higher gross margins (48–52%) vs. AMAT (42–48%) by focusing on lower-volume, higher-ASP specialty segments. TYE's partnership with TSMC on advanced node tools creates competitive threat in AMAT's core market. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 industry overview and competitive analysis.

competitors.name: Novellus Systems (acquired by LRCX 2012)
competitors.relationshipNote: Historical competitor in chemical-mechanical planarization (CMP) tools; acquired by Lam Research in 2012 for $3.3B. Novellus' CMP technology was complementary to AMAT's deposition/etch tools; LRCX's acquisition consolidated CMP market share and created bundled tool offerings that compete with AMAT's standalone tools. This acquisition signaled LRCX's strategy to build integrated process-tool portfolios. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 competitive analysis and historical filings.

competitors.name: Mattson Technology (acquired by AMAT 2013)
competitors.relationshipNote: Historical competitor in rapid thermal processing (RTP) and thermal processing tools; acquired by AMAT in 2013 for $280M. Mattson's RTP technology was complementary to AMAT's deposition tools; acquisition expanded AMAT's thermal processing portfolio and reduced competitive threat. This acquisition signaled AMAT's strategy to consolidate process-tool capabilities. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 and 8-K filings.

regulators.name: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: Primary financial regulator; AMAT files 10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, and DEF14A with SEC. SEC reviews AMAT's disclosure of customer concentration risk, China revenue exposure, and export control compliance. SEC's focus on cybersecurity disclosure (2023 rules) and climate risk disclosure (proposed rules) creates new compliance obligations for AMAT. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A risk factors and quarterly filings.

regulators.name: U.S. Department of Commerce — Bureau of Industry and Security
regulators.relationshipNote: Export control regulator; BIS enforces Export Administration Regulations (EAR) on AMAT's equipment sales to China and other restricted countries. BIS restrictions on advanced semiconductor equipment (2022–24) have reduced AMAT's China revenue by $2–3B annually. AMAT must obtain export licenses for China-bound tools; license denials create revenue uncertainty. BIS Entity List additions (SMIC, CXMT, others) restrict AMAT's ability to sell to Chinese customers. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A China risk factors and 8-K filings on export control announcements.

regulators.name: U.S. Federal Trade Commission
regulators.relationshipNote: Antitrust regulator; FTC monitors AMAT's competitive position and potential antitrust violations. AMAT's market dominance in deposition/etch tools (40–45% share) creates antitrust scrutiny. FTC has historically reviewed AMAT's acquisitions (e.g., Mattson 2013, Varian 2011) for competitive impact. FTC's focus on semiconductor supply chain resilience (2021–23) has elevated AMAT's regulatory profile. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A risk factors.

regulators.name: Taiwan Economic and Trade Office (TETO) / U.S. State Department
regulators.relationshipNote: Geopolitical regulator; U.S. State Department and Taiwan relations affect AMAT's ability to sell to TSMC and other Taiwan customers. U.S.–China tensions and potential Taiwan military conflict create binary downside scenario for AMAT revenue (TSMC represents 30–35% of revenue). State Department's Taiwan Policy Act and semiconductor supply chain resilience initiatives create regulatory uncertainty. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A risk factors and 8-K filings on geopolitical events.

regulators.name: California Air Resources Board (CARB) / U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
regulators.relationshipNote: Environmental regulator; EPA and CARB regulate AMAT's manufacturing facilities (Santa Clara, California) for air quality, water discharge, and hazardous waste. AMAT's equipment uses perfluorinated compounds (PFCs) and other hazardous materials; EPA restrictions on PFCs create manufacturing compliance costs. CARB's California emissions standards affect AMAT's facility operations. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1A environmental risk factors.

auditor.name: Deloitte & Touche LLP
auditor.relationshipNote: Big-Four auditor; Deloitte audits AMAT's consolidated financial statements and internal controls over financial reporting (SOX 404 compliance). Deloitte's audit scope includes revenue recognition (customer concentration, contract terms), inventory valuation (obsolescence risk), and goodwill impairment (acquisitions). Deloitte's audit opinion is unqualified as of FY2024. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 8 financial statements and Item 9A internal controls.

capitalProviders.name: JPMorgan Chase & Co.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Primary lender; JPMorgan is AMAT's lead bank on revolving credit facility ($3B committed, undrawn as of FY2024) and has underwritten AMAT's bond offerings. JPMorgan's credit analysts monitor AMAT's leverage ratio, interest coverage, and capex intensity. JPMorgan's semiconductor sector expertise and relationships with AMAT's customers (TSMC, Samsung, Intel) create information advantage. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 7 debt schedule and quarterly filings.

capitalProviders.name: Bank of America Merrill Lynch
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Secondary lender; BofA is part of AMAT's syndicated credit facility and has underwritten AMAT's bond offerings. BofA's equity research team covers AMAT and publishes quarterly earnings estimates and price targets. BofA's investment banking team advises AMAT on M&A and capital structure optimization. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 7 debt schedule and quarterly filings.

capitalProviders.name: Vanguard Group, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Largest institutional shareholder; Vanguard holds ~7–8% of AMAT shares as of FY2024. Vanguard's passive index funds (S&P 500, Total Stock Market) hold AMAT as a core technology holding. Vanguard's active engagement on ESG and governance issues influences AMAT's board composition and executive compensation. Disclosed in AMAT DEF14A proxy statement and Vanguard's public holdings disclosures.

capitalProviders.name: BlackRock, Inc.
capitalProviders.relationshipNote: Second-largest institutional shareholder; BlackRock holds ~6–7% of AMAT shares as of FY2024. BlackRock's passive index funds and active equity strategies hold AMAT as a core technology holding. BlackRock's engagement on climate risk, board diversity, and executive compensation influences AMAT's governance. Disclosed in AMAT DEF14A proxy statement and BlackRock's public holdings disclosures.

executiveTeam.name: Gary E. Dickerson
executiveTeam.title: President and Chief Executive Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: CEO since 2012; led AMAT through 2015–16 capex cycle recovery, 2018 peak, and 2022–23 downturn. Dickerson's strategic focus on advanced-node tools and customer diversification has maintained AMAT's market leadership. Dickerson's compensation is tied to revenue growth, gross margin, and free cash flow targets. Disclosed in AMAT DEF14A proxy statement and quarterly earnings calls.

executiveTeam.name: Brice Hill
executiveTeam.title: Chief Financial Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: CFO since 2021; responsible for AMAT's financial planning, capital allocation, and investor relations. Hill's focus on free cash flow generation and debt reduction has improved AMAT's balance sheet. Hill's quarterly earnings guidance and commentary on gross margin trends directly influence AMAT's stock price. Disclosed in AMAT DEF14A proxy statement and quarterly earnings calls.

executiveTeam.name: Omkaram Nalamasu
executiveTeam.title: Chief Technology Officer
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: CTO since 2018; responsible for AMAT's R&D roadmap and technology development strategy. Nalamasu's focus on advanced-node process tools (EUV, high-NA lithography enablement) has maintained AMAT's competitive position vs. Lam Research. Nalamasu's patent portfolio (1000+ patents) and customer design-win announcements signal AMAT's technology leadership. Disclosed in AMAT 10-K Item 1 R&D overview and quarterly earnings calls.

executiveTeam.name: Michael R. Splinter
executiveTeam.title: Chairman of the Board
executiveTeam.relationshipNote: Chairman since 2012; former CEO (2002–2012). Splinter's board leadership has overseen AMAT's strategic acquisitions (Varian 2011, Mattson 2013) and capital allocation decisions. Splinter's relationships with AMAT's major customers and competitors provide strategic insight. Disclosed in AMAT DEF14A proxy statement and board committee disclosures.

marketSignals.name: SEMI Semiconductor Equipment Billings Index
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Monthly index of semiconductor equipment billings (AMAT, LRCX, Tokyo Electron, others); leading indicator of fab capex spending 1–2 quarters forward. SEMI billings index peaked at 130+ in 2021–22 and declined to 70–80 in 2023; recovery to 100+ would signal renewed capex cycle. AMAT's billings typically represent 35–40% of SEMI index. Disclosed in SEMI public reports and AMAT quarterly earnings calls.

marketSignals.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association (TSIA) Fab Utilization Rate
marketSignals.relationshipNote: Monthly fab utilization rate for Taiwan foundries (TSMC, UMC, MediaTek); leading indicator of AMAT orders 2–3 quarters forward. Taiwan fab utilization peaked at 90%+ in 2021–22 and declined to 60–70% in 2023; recovery to 80%+ would signal renewed capex cycle. TSMC's utilization rate is most relevant to AMAT (TSMC represents 30–35% of revenue). Disclosed in TSIA public reports and AMAT quarterly earnings calls.
